Their offer? A system with familiarities appreciated by developers and online services welcomed by users.</p><p>Please note that to keep consistency with other sources, this article separates storage units between the metric prefix (i.e. megabytes or ‘MB’) and the standardised binary prefix (i.e. mebibytes or ‘MiB’), thus:</p><ul><li>1 MB = 1000 KB</li><li>1 MiB = 1024 KiB</li></ul><p>… and so forth.</p><h3 id="reading-tips">Reading tips</h3><p>Some months after writing this, I’ve realised this is one of the densest write-ups I have done. There’s just a lot of stuff happening inside the Xbox and I have tried to mention most of it.</p><p>Now, if you’re really interested in understanding this system but find this article difficult to follow, my advice to you is: <strong>Take your time</strong>, the article is not going anywhere. Focus on what you like, read at your own pace, check out the links on the ‘Sources’ section for support and finally, don’t put pressure on yourself, there’s no exam!</p><hr><h2 id="cpu">CPU</h2><p>The processor included in this console is a slightly customised version of the famous <strong>Intel Pentium III</strong> (an off-the-shelf CPU for computers) running at <strong>733 MHz</strong>. With this, one can assume this console is just a PC behind the scenes… I won’t tell you the answer, but I promise that at the end of the article you will be able to reach your own conclusion.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/cpu.758eb12ff9bcad8e049fefdd9e96393576a1654dc5bde2a788011de8fcd7a9b9.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/cpu.758eb12ff9bcad8e049fefdd9e96393576a1654dc5bde2a788011de8fcd7a9b9_hu_6fcc0d7a1a16338b.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/cpu.758eb12ff9bcad8e049fefdd9e96393576a1654dc5bde2a788011de8fcd7a9b9_hu_123691e7b1697224.webp 600w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="600" height="511" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/cpu.758eb12ff9bcad8e049fefdd9e96393576a1654dc5bde2a788011de8fcd7a9b9.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The Intel Pentium III package on the Xbox’s motherboard.</figcaption></figure><p>Anyhow, Pentiums, along with other lines of CPUs designed and manufactured by Intel, were incredibly popular in the computer market. Such was Intel’s market share that they became the de-facto reference point for quality: As a typical user, if you wanted a good computer and had the budget, you only had to look for <em>something</em> carrying an Intel CPU. We all know by now that there are more factors involved, but that’s what the marketing guys at Intel managed to project.</p><h3 id="technical-information">Technical information</h3><p>Now that we positioned Intel on the map, let’s go back to the topic of this console. During my research, I was expecting to find documentation with the level of depth as other CPUs (MIPS, SuperH, ARM, etc), but instead, I stumbled across an excessive amount of marketing terms that only diverted my search. So, for this article, I came up with a structure to organise all the necessary information which will help to understand how this CPU works. Furthermore, I will try to introduce some terminology that Intel used to brand this CPU.</p><p>Having said that, let us take a look:</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-1-1-branding-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-1-1-branding">Branding</a></li><li id="tab-1-2-the-isa-link"><a href="#tab-1-2-the-isa">The ISA</a></li><li id="tab-1-3-the-microarchitecture-link"><a href="#tab-1-3-the-microarchitecture">The Microarchitecture</a></li><li id="tab-1-4-cisc-or-risc-link"><a href="#tab-1-4-cisc-or-risc">CISC or RISC</a></li><li id="tab-1-5-the-core-link"><a href="#tab-1-5-the-core">The Core</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-1-1-branding"><h4 id="tab-1-1-branding" class="tab-title">Branding</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/cpu/branding.4586322b0f315b19e6b34ec6a1c3ca139d587ec851b88cd4236a1365aa8e7295.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="483" height="321" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/cpu/branding.4586322b0f315b19e6b34ec6a1c3ca139d587ec851b88cd4236a1365aa8e7295.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">How this study is organised.</figcaption></figure><p>First things first, the Xbox’s CPU is identified as a <strong>Pentium III</strong>. So what does this mean? Back then (early noughties), the Pentium series represented the next generation of CPUs. They were the ‘new high-end’ that grouped all the fancy technology that made computers super-fast, plus it helped buyers decide which CPU they had to buy if they wanted <em>the best of the best</em>.</p><p>Pentium III replaced Pentium II, which in turn replaced the original Pentium. Moreover, when the first Pentium came out, it replaced the 80486, which in turn replaced the 80386… You get the idea. What matters is that ‘Pentium’ is mainly a brand name, it’s not directly associated with its inner workings. Therefore, we must go deeper!</p><p>To dive further and not get lost in the way, I have catalogued the information into three sections which combined, make up the chip. The first the <strong>Instruction Set Architecture</strong> or ‘ISA’ (the group of instructions used to command the CPU), <strong>Microarchitecture</strong> (how is the ISA implemented in silicon) and the <strong>Core</strong> (what set of components are used to package the microarchitecture to form the specific CPU model).</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-2-the-isa">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-2-the-isa"><h4 id="tab-1-2-the-isa" class="tab-title">The ISA</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/photos/i386.d018e3c80bf7921aa8095d03d0e4f812f2f7db292f3e1c42cdda0dbc717ac7d0.webp"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/photos/i386.d018e3c80bf7921aa8095d03d0e4f812f2f7db292f3e1c42cdda0dbc717ac7d0.webp"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="774" height="645" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/photos/i386.d018e3c80bf7921aa8095d03d0e4f812f2f7db292f3e1c42cdda0dbc717ac7d0_hu_da8c8a61e799f53f.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">An Intel 80386 (1985), or compatible, was the minimum requirement for mid-90s applications.</figcaption></figure><p>Indeed, once I mention ‘Intel’ it’s a matter of time before I introduce the famous <strong>x86</strong>, its instruction set.</p><p>The first form of x86 debuted with the release of the <strong>Intel 8086</strong> in 1978, a 16-bit CPU. Afterwards, the ISA was constantly expanded with more instructions as more Intel CPUs were released (80186, 80286 and so on) <sup id="bibref:1"><a href="#bib:cpu-thompson" role="doc-biblioref">[1]</a></sup>. Consequently, x86 started to fragment as more ground-breaking features were added (i.e. ‘protected mode’ and ‘long mode’). To tackle this, modern x86 applications commonly target the 80386 ISA (also called <strong>IA-32</strong> or <strong>i386</strong>) as a baseline, which among other things, operates in a 32-bit environment.</p><p>Subsequently, Intel enhanced the IA-32 with the use of <strong>extensions</strong>, meaning the new functions may or may not be included in an IA-32 CPU. Programs query the CPU to check if a specific enhancement is present. The Xbox’s CPU includes two extensions:</p><ul><li><strong>MMX</strong> (Multimedia Extension): Adds 57 SIMD instructions and 8 64-bit registers (integers only) that can speed up vector operations.</li><li><strong>SSE</strong> (Streaming SIMD extension): Another SIMD-type extension that addresses the criticism of MMX (lack of floating-point support and unable to use the floating-point unit in parallel). It adds 56 new instructions and eight 128-bit registers (called ‘XMM’) that hold four 32-bit <code>floats</code>.</li></ul><p>The good news is that, since the console will always have the same CPU, programmers can optimise their code to exploit these extensions as they will always be present.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-1-branding">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-3-the-microarchitecture">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-3-the-microarchitecture"><h4 id="tab-1-3-the-microarchitecture" class="tab-title">The Microarchitecture</h4><p>When it comes to building a circuit that can interpret x86 instructions, Intel has come up with so many different designs for their CPUs. Some designs were featured with the release of a new Pentium Series (i.e. Pentium 4) while others were featured when Intel released an ‘enhanced’ version of a Pentium (such as the ‘Pentium Pro’). Nevertheless, since the release of the first Pentium, the CPU model and microarchitecture no longer carry the same name. For example, the 80486 uses the 80486 microarchitecture (and no other), however, the original Pentium has the ‘P5’ microarchitecture.</p><p>Now, the Xbox CPU, along with the rest of Pentium III processors, use the <strong>P6 Microarchitecture</strong> (also known as ‘i686’). This is the 6th generation (counting from the 8086) which features:</p><ul><li>A <em>massive</em> <strong>14-stage pipeline</strong>: Meaning up to 14 instructions can be processed in parallel. On the other side, individual instructions may take a lot more cycles to complete. See <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#tab-2-1-the-core">a previous explanation</a>.</li><li><strong>Out-of-order execution</strong>: If possible, the CPU re-orders the sequence of instructions to increase efficiency and performance.</li><li><strong>Dynamic execution</strong>: Since the P6 is an out-of-order and <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/dreamcast/#cpu">superscalar</a> design. The traditional <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#the-powerpc-gekko">branch predictor</a> is now combined with other techniques (‘speculative execution’ and ‘data-flow analysis’) to take advantage of the new capabilities. In doing so, it reduces pipeline stalling even further.</li></ul><p>Having said that, take a closer look at these features. It so happens they are very similar to <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#the-powerpc-gekko">previous consoles</a>, however, the other CPUs are very different in terms of design compared to Intel ones. Historically, one could argue that the design of the x86 would’ve never allowed Intel to produce, let’s say, a pipelined CPU. Yet they managed to do so, so let us see why…</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-2-the-isa">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-4-cisc-or-risc">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-4-cisc-or-risc"><h4 id="tab-1-4-cisc-or-risc" class="tab-title">CISC or RISC</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/photos/pentiumpro.85313ffad1b5ece6add0b66c57389c36799f3a3e549ad397f862c3b1aaaf0fbe.webp"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/photos/pentiumpro.85313ffad1b5ece6add0b66c57389c36799f3a3e549ad397f862c3b1aaaf0fbe_hu_7f03e077b5797a51.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/photos/pentiumpro.85313ffad1b5ece6add0b66c57389c36799f3a3e549ad397f862c3b1aaaf0fbe_hu_f981404e442a6ca7.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/photos/pentiumpro.85313ffad1b5ece6add0b66c57389c36799f3a3e549ad397f862c3b1aaaf0fbe_hu_65d8afc7c5a114df.webp 900w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="900" height="757" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/photos/pentiumpro.85313ffad1b5ece6add0b66c57389c36799f3a3e549ad397f862c3b1aaaf0fbe_hu_cf0b8fac5bee5813.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Intel’s Pentium Pro (1995) debuted the P6 microarchitecture, bridging the gap between CISC and RISC advancements in the x86 world. This came as a surprise to many - particularly those who believed x86’s days were numbered.</figcaption></figure><p>The competition happens to feature CPUs designed around the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#tab-1-1-a-bit-of-history">RISC guidelines</a>, whereas Intel’s x86 is not, thereby being placed in the <strong>CISC</strong> group. RISC CPUs are known for having an intentionally simplified design compared to CISC CPUs. This includes, for instance, implementing a <strong>load–store architecture</strong>, which only provides instructions that operate values from registers (as opposed to operating directly from memory).</p><p>One of the advantages of RISC processors is that their simplistic approach enables its CPUs to be designed with a modular sense, which in turn can be exploited to improve performance with parallelism techniques. This is why we have seen CPUs like MIPS and PowerPC debuting pipeline stages, superscalar designs, out-of-order execution, branch prediction, etc. On the other side, CISC processors predate RISC ones and the former aimed to solve different needs. Consequently, their designs are not as flexible as RISC CPUs.</p><p>Back to the original question, the P6 is an interesting design, because while this CPU only understands a CISC instruction set (x86), a subset of its opcodes is interpreted using <strong>microcode</strong>. Most importantly, the unit that executes microcode <strong>is built around the load-store model</strong> <sup id="bibref:2"><a href="#bib:cpu-gwennap" role="doc-biblioref">[2]</a></sup>. This is because the P6 architecture was authored by the former engineers of the <strong>Intel i960</strong> (a once-promising RISC CPU by Intel). All in all, this has enabled Intel to gain similar advantages to RISC processors without breaking compatibility with the historic x86 ISA. It’s fair to say that as time passed by, terms like ‘CISC’ and ‘RISC’ have become too ambiguous to categorise any modern CPU.</p><p>As a side note, microcode is already embedded in the silicon but it can be patched, allowing Intel to fix its CPUs after production whenever a bug or a security vulnerability is discovered. If you have read previous articles (i.e. <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/">N64</a> or <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-2/">PS2</a>), bear in mind that Intel’s microcode is <strong>not publicly accessible</strong> (let alone documented) and Intel is its sole ‘maintainer’.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-3-the-microarchitecture">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-5-the-core">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-5-the-core"><h4 id="tab-1-5-the-core" class="tab-title">The Core</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/cpu/core.9cd5ed4bf1554798a5170952751e070ed20bdb4364df475bf19c4ac55cc17133.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="422" height="527" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/cpu/core.9cd5ed4bf1554798a5170952751e070ed20bdb4364df475bf19c4ac55cc17133.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The Coppermine design.</figcaption></figure><p>Intel shipped numerous chips that implemented the P6 microarchitecture. The Xbox includes one model called <strong>Coppermine</strong>. It was branded as the second revision of the Pentium III (replacing the ‘Katmai’ core) and features the following components:</p><ul><li><strong>32 KiB L1</strong> cache: Divided between 16 KiB for instructions and 16 KiB for data.</li><li>Integrated <strong>128 KiB L2</strong> cache: This is <em>odd</em> since the off-the-shelf Coppermine has 256 KiB of L2 <sup id="bibref:3"><a href="#bib:cpu-anand" role="doc-biblioref">[3]</a></sup>. In fact, the Coppermine128 (found in the Intel ‘Celeron’ brand, the low-end Pentium alternative) has the same amount of L2 <sup id="bibref:4"><a href="#bib:cpu-shvets" role="doc-biblioref">[4]</a></sup>. Hence, this was probably done to reduce manufacturing costs and keep this console at a competitive price.</li><li>133 MHz <strong>Front-side bus</strong>: This is the bus that connects the L2 cache with the memory controller, we’ll see more about it later on.<ul><li>Intel names it ‘Front-side bus’ to distinguish it from another bus that connects L2 (external cache) with L1 (internal cache). The latter bus is called ‘Back-side bus’… and it’s an unfortunate name to use in the UK.</li></ul></li></ul><p>Coppermine also adds two ‘enhancements’ over their original implementation of L2 cache, these are the <strong>Advanced Transfer Cache</strong> and the <strong>Advanced System Buffering</strong>. To sum them up, L2 cache is on-chip and their buses are wider, which helps to reduce possible bottlenecks in the Front-side bus.</p><p>Finally, the chip uses the ‘Micro-PGA2’ socket fit on the motherboard, but like any other console, the Xbox has it soldered with a Ball Grid Array or ‘BGA’.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-4-cisc-or-risc">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="p6-and-the-end-of-pentium-numbers">P6 and the end of Pentium numbers</h3><p>Here’s a bit more history. After the years of the P6, Intel planned to succeed it with the ‘NetBurst’ microarchitecture (featured in the Pentium IV). However, the line of succession also ended there. Even though NetBurst implemented many contemporary techniques <sup id="bibref:5"><a href="#bib:cpu-netburst" role="doc-biblioref">[5]</a></sup>, it also suffered from excessive power consumption, heat emission (an average of 85 W <sup id="bibref:6"><a href="#bib:cpu-pentium4" role="doc-biblioref">[6]</a></sup>) and scalability issues - all of which impeded the design from being continued any further.</p><p>Consequently, this prompted an Intel team in Israel to revisit their low-powered P6 CPU - the ‘Pentium M’ - and develop a more powerful successor. The first result was the <strong>Yonah</strong> core, a slight improvement of the P6 design branded as <strong>Core Solo</strong> or <strong>Core Duo</strong>. With it, power dissipation dropped to reasonable numbers (between 27 W <sup id="bibref:7"><a href="#bib:cpu-coresolo" role="doc-biblioref">[7]</a></sup> and 31 W <sup id="bibref:8"><a href="#bib:cpu-coreduo" role="doc-biblioref">[8]</a></sup>, depending on the variant). Months later, the follow-up <strong>Core</strong> microarchitecture became the flagship successor of P6 (and NetBurst) and, confusingly enough, reached the shelves in the form of the <strong>Core 2</strong> CPU line. Over the years, subsequent microarchitectures improved on many aspects, but they also managed to re-incorporate forgotten elements from NetBurst without repeating the same mistakes.</p><p>On a curious note, I wonder if the naming of the Yonah core is meant as a metaphor for the Book of Jonah, particularly connecting the event where the prophet, in the end, managed to correct his path to save the city of Nineveh. Though it’s also possible I’m overthinking this.</p><h3 id="motherboard-architecture">Motherboard architecture</h3><p>At some point in the history of the PC, motherboards grew so much in complexity that new designs had to be developed from the ground up to efficiently tackle emerging needs.</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/cpu/motherboard.6c4ba9a973d019cfba1b491416137efdd201ca5a62b92eeac6ae953e3149ea2f.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="736" height="596" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/cpu/motherboard.6c4ba9a973d019cfba1b491416137efdd201ca5a62b92eeac6ae953e3149ea2f.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Overview of Xbox Motherboard.</figcaption></figure><p>The new standard developed relied on two dedicated chips to handle most of the motherboard functions. These chips are:</p><ul><li>The <strong>Northbridge</strong>: Serves as a memory controller and interfaces the GPU.</li><li>The <strong>Southbridge</strong>: Interfaces the rest of I/O (i.e. USB, ATA/SATA, PCI, etc)</li></ul><p>The combination of these chips is called <strong>chipset</strong> and they are important enough to condition the capabilities and performance of a motherboard. The Xbox, being so close to a PC, includes two chips as well: The <strong>NV2A</strong>, a combination of Northbridge and GPU; and the <strong>MCPX</strong> which handles the rest of I/O.</p></div><p>Both chips are interconnected using a specialised bus called the <strong>HyperTransport</strong>. It’s worth pointing out that some PC motherboards also included this technology, just with a different brand (<em>nForce MCP-D</em>).</p><h3 id="memory-layout">Memory layout</h3><p>The Xbox includes a total of <strong>64 MiB of DDR SDRAM</strong>, this type of RAM is very fast compared to what the competition offers. However, it’s also shared across all components of this system. Hence, once more, we find ourselves in front of another <strong>unified memory architecture</strong> or ‘UMA’ layout.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/cpu/memory.0da9d3e4593cad8958d087b702d033ce52343df7ea0749bd970c218ed5f0be08.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="674" height="308" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/cpu/memory.0da9d3e4593cad8958d087b702d033ce52343df7ea0749bd970c218ed5f0be08.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Representation of the switching network. GPU uses two banks while the CPU uses a different one, reducing contention in the process.</figcaption></figure><p>We have previously seen how <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-2/#preventing-past-mishaps">troublesome</a> this design can be sometimes. Nonetheless, programs can address this issue by spreading their data between different banks of memory. NV2A implements a <strong>switching network</strong> that enables different units (CPU, GPU, etc) to concurrently access them <sup id="bibref:9"><a href="#bib:cpu-huang" role="doc-biblioref">[9]</a></sup> <sup id="bibref:10"><a href="#bib:cpu-informit" role="doc-biblioref">[10]</a></sup>.</p><p>Furthermore, the console features an internal hard disk, and it <em>so happens</em> to be set up with three partitions of 750 MiB each reserved for temporary storage. The CPU can offload some of its data from main RAM, then upload it back whenever it’s needed. Bear in mind this is a manual process and does not involve virtual RAM.</p><hr><h2 id="graphics">Graphics</h2><p>As we’ve seen before, the graphics processor resides in the NV2A chip and, just like MCPX, it is manufactured by Nvidia.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/gpu.0df4e82a465b263df02130b8718fe2c5382e1182e8f8ae113713146a45f6d035.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/gpu.0df4e82a465b263df02130b8718fe2c5382e1182e8f8ae113713146a45f6d035_hu_b4bed34ac216ae77.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/gpu.0df4e82a465b263df02130b8718fe2c5382e1182e8f8ae113713146a45f6d035_hu_f620c652def365a7.webp 700w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="700" height="560" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/gpu.0df4e82a465b263df02130b8718fe2c5382e1182e8f8ae113713146a45f6d035.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The Nvidia NV2A package on the Xbox’s motherboard.</figcaption></figure><p>This company has been in the graphics business for a long time, their <em>GeForce</em> series are one of the most popular GPU brands in the computer market, directly competing against the Radeon series from ArtX/ATI. Overall, this provides good leverage on the quality of graphics found in the Xbox, considering it’s Microsoft’s first attempt in the console market.</p><p>It all seems reasonable, but was it <em>really</em> a certain decision to make back then? It’s easy to rely on present history to find out why Microsoft chose Nvidia over other popular brands from the time (3dfx, PowerVR, S3, etc), but if we read more about the competition back then, the panorama of options made it much more complex.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/halo.e7f4908e958ec058ef5ebde3d20cc139379a9547600e1d5f845f3c85498d5fed.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/halo.e7f4908e958ec058ef5ebde3d20cc139379a9547600e1d5f845f3c85498d5fed_hu_7dda8d73dec38f3c.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/halo.e7f4908e958ec058ef5ebde3d20cc139379a9547600e1d5f845f3c85498d5fed_hu_2f1974e05f59088a.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/halo.e7f4908e958ec058ef5ebde3d20cc139379a9547600e1d5f845f3c85498d5fed_hu_2d11a9bfb35a1362.webp 1280w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1280" height="720" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/halo.e7f4908e958ec058ef5ebde3d20cc139379a9547600e1d5f845f3c85498d5fed.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Halo (2001) running on the Xbox in 720p mode.</figcaption></figure><p>For instance, 3dfx’s popular ‘Voodoo 2’ series had ~70% of the market share in the PC market by the end of the 90s <sup id="bibref:11"><a href="#bib:graphics-ign" role="doc-biblioref">[11]</a></sup>, while Nvidia was struggling to promote adoption of the new ‘GeForce 256’ (the first of the GeForce series). After this, Microsoft’s choice now sounds more like a risk than a safe bet, but as we know by now, this risk eventually paid off.</p><blockquote><p>Nvidia was NOT the #1 player they are now, in 1999. They were in trouble. The new GeForce architecture was still young and lots of people didn’t like it. Now it seems forgone. But you’d need to research that history to know that, and why I had to fight to use it. I was right but I didn’t know I was right; I was very worried.</p><p>– <cite>Seamus Blackley (Co-author of the original Xbox)</cite></p></blockquote><p>In the following section, we’ll examine the inner workings of this chip. Now, I’m afraid we find ourselves mixed in a lot of terminology and marketing terms just like the CPU section, but fear not! I’ll start with the basics.</p><h3 id="architecture-and-design">Architecture and design</h3><p>The GPU core found on the NV2A is based on the popular ‘GeForce3’ series of GPUs <sup id="bibref:12"><a href="#bib:graphics-mslusarz" role="doc-biblioref">[12]</a></sup> <sup id="bibref:13"><a href="#bib:graphics-g3arch" role="doc-biblioref">[13]</a></sup>, it’s also referred to as <strong>NV20</strong> in Nvidia’s technical documents.</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/gpu/pipeline.063375a98e614973919523251b419124705ce98e64e192bbd2b4ace91570f3d8.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="608" height="481" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/gpu/pipeline.063375a98e614973919523251b419124705ce98e64e192bbd2b4ace91570f3d8.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Pipeline design of the NV2A.</figcaption></figure><p>Please note that, while the pipeline of the Xbox’s GPU is based on the NV20 architecture, the NV2A has some modifications that are not compatible with the rest of the NV20 series (most importantly, it has been adapted to work in a UMA environment).</p><p>The units analysed contain a lot more features that go beyond the scope of this article, so I recommend checking out the sources/references if this section catches your attention. Also, since graphics-related terminology is constantly evolving (which can lead to some confusion), I’ve decided to rely on the terms used by Microsoft/Nvidia during the years of the Xbox, so remember this if you plan to read more graphics-related articles from other sources.</p></div><p>Having said that, let’s take a look at how frames are drawn in the Xbox. Some explanations are very similar to GameCube’s <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#graphics">Flipper</a>, so you may benefit from reading that article as well in case you struggle to follow this one.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-2-1-commands-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-2-1-commands">Commands</a></li><li id="tab-2-2-vertex-link"><a href="#tab-2-2-vertex">Vertex</a></li><li id="tab-2-3-pixel-link"><a href="#tab-2-3-pixel">Pixel</a></li><li id="tab-2-4-post-processing-link"><a href="#tab-2-4-post-processing">Post-processing</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-2-1-commands"><h4 id="tab-2-1-commands" class="tab-title">Commands</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/gpu/commands.52fc59a8cb96cc12fad2ef5fc0e7df1509aca825ebe3403b53487d5e913b58de.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="586" height="242" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/gpu/commands.52fc59a8cb96cc12fad2ef5fc0e7df1509aca825ebe3403b53487d5e913b58de.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Commands stage.</figcaption></figure><p>First and foremost is explaining how the GPU can receive commands from the CPU. For that, the GPU contains a command processor called <strong>PFIFO</strong> that effectively fetches and processes graphics commands (called <strong>Pushbuffer</strong>) in a FIFO manner, the unpacked commands are subsequently delivered to the <strong>PGRAPH</strong> (the block in charge of graphics processing) and other engines.</p><p>Like Flipper, geometry doesn’t have to be embedded in the command. PGRAPH provides many ways to submit graphics data. For instance, the CPU can allocate a buffer in RAM containing vertex data and then instruct the GPU to fetch them from that location. This approach can be efficient, as it prevents sending duplicated geometry.</p><p>The next explanations happen in PGRAPH.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-2-vertex">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-2-vertex"><h4 id="tab-2-2-vertex" class="tab-title">Vertex</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/gpu/vertex.d7e919c3caabcf1a6732aaeb7ab95629e9d30ca878b54ba7f0b1daa634a8c7ed.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="626" height="481" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/gpu/vertex.d7e919c3caabcf1a6732aaeb7ab95629e9d30ca878b54ba7f0b1daa634a8c7ed.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Vertex stage.</figcaption></figure><p>This is an interesting section for this GPU in particular. At this stage, the GPU provides the ability to apply vertex transformations to our geometry. We’ve already seen this feature with Flipper, but unlike that GPU, this one uses a <strong>programmable engine</strong>. This means that developers may specify which vertex operations are performed and how, as opposed to relying on a predefined program. Although, the NV2A can also operate in ‘fixed’ mode, if required.</p><p>This stage is handled by a <strong>Vertex Unit</strong> and the NV2A features <strong>two of them</strong>. Each can load a program containing up to 136 instructions (also called <strong>microcode</strong>). This program is referred to as <strong>vertex program</strong> and it’s loaded at runtime. A vertex program can perform the following operations <sup id="bibref:14"><a href="#bib:graphics-koppelman" role="doc-biblioref">[14]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li><strong>Arithmetic operations</strong> (i.e. addition, multiplication, minimum, etc).<ul><li>This includes ‘helper functions’ to assist graphics-related tasks, such as dot product.</li></ul></li><li><strong>Vertex Swizzling</strong> (Rearrangement and/or duplication).</li></ul><p>In a nutshell, the vertex unit processes vertices by manipulating them in its registers. In other words, once the program is loaded, 16 read-only registers (called ‘input registers’) are initialised with the attributes of a vertex (each vector contains four components). Afterwards, the unit performs the set of operations (instructed by the program) using the input registers. Furthermore, 12 writable registers and up to 196 constants are provided to assist the computation. Finally, the resulting vertex is stored in another block of 11 writable registers (each one limited to a specific purpose), which are passed on to the next stage. This process is repeated for every vertex received.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-1-commands">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-3-pixel">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-3-pixel"><h4 id="tab-2-3-pixel" class="tab-title">Pixel</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/gpu/pixel.5b9f394c65582c778c87df1861b67d3f0f77d7297659c83fe203d05245a1b82c.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="723" height="527" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/gpu/pixel.5b9f394c65582c778c87df1861b67d3f0f77d7297659c83fe203d05245a1b82c.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Fragment/Pixel stage.</figcaption></figure><p>At this stage, vertices are transformed into pixels. The process starts with a rasteriser that generates pixels to draw each triangle. The NV2A’s rasteriser can generate four pixels per cycle.</p><p>Afterwards, <strong>4 texture shaders</strong> are used to fetch textures from memory <sup id="bibref:15"><a href="#bib:graphics-domine" role="doc-biblioref">[15]</a></sup>, these also offer to automatically apply anisotropic filtering, mipmapping and <strong>shadow buffering</strong>. The latter one is used to test whether a pixel is visible or overshadowed by the lighting source, so the correct colour can be applied. At this point, the GPU also offers to perform clipping and an early <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#modern-visible-surface-determination">Z-test</a> (the NV2A compresses the Z-buffer four times its original size to save bandwidth, contributing to a lot of performance improvements).</p><p>The resulting pixels are stored in a <strong>set of shared registers</strong> and then cycled through <strong>8 register combiners</strong>, where each one applies arithmetic operations on them. This process is <strong>programmable</strong> with the use of <strong>pixel shaders</strong> (another type of program executed by the GPU) <sup id="bibref:16"><a href="#bib:graphics-wasson" role="doc-biblioref">[16]</a></sup>. At each cycle, each combiner receives RGBA values (RGB + Alpha) from the register set <sup id="bibref:17"><a href="#bib:graphics-spitzer" role="doc-biblioref">[17]</a></sup>. Then, based on the operation set by the shader, it will operate the values and write back the result. Finally, a larger amount of values are sent to the <strong>final combiner</strong> which can exclusively blend specular colours and/or fog.</p><p>Register combiners are programmable in a similar nature to the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#tab-3-3-texture">Texture Environment Unit</a>. That is, by altering its registers with a specific combination of settings. In the case of the Xbox, the PFIFO reads pushbuffers to set up PGRAPH, which includes the register combiners and texture shaders.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-2-vertex">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-4-post-processing">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-4-post-processing"><h4 id="tab-2-4-post-processing" class="tab-title">Post-processing</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/gpu/postprocessing.52fc59a8cb96cc12fad2ef5fc0e7df1509aca825ebe3403b53487d5e913b58de.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="586" height="242" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/gpu/postprocessing.52fc59a8cb96cc12fad2ef5fc0e7df1509aca825ebe3403b53487d5e913b58de.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Post-processing stage.</figcaption></figure><p>Before the pixels are written to the frame-buffer, the NV2A contains four dedicated engines called <strong>Raster Output Unit</strong> or ‘ROP’ which perform necessary tests (alpha, depth and stencil) using allocated blocks in main memory. Finally, batches of pixels (four per cycle) are written back only if they pass these tests.</p><p>Moreover, the frame-buffer can be anti-aliased using a technique called <strong>multisampling</strong> <sup id="bibref:18"><a href="#bib:graphics-geforce3" role="doc-biblioref">[18]</a></sup>. Essentially, this technique samples the edges of polygons multiple times with different offsets added in the process. Afterwards, all samples are averaged to form the anti-aliased image. This approach replaced the previous (and more resource-hungry) anti-aliasing function called ‘supersampling’, used by previous Nvidia GPUs.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-3-pixel">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="the-importance-of-programmability">The importance of programmability</h3><p>I find it pivotal to emphasise the significance of the new programmability model that Nvidia provided to developers. Years ago, most of the graphics pipeline was computed by the CPU, leaving the GPU to accelerate rasterising operations. With the introduction of ‘shaders’ (referring to both pixel shaders and vertex programs), programmers can take advantage of the resources of the GPU to accelerate many computations in the pipeline, offloading a great amount of work from the CPU.</p><p>The concept of ‘shaders’ was introduced by <strong>Pixar</strong> in 1989 as a method to extend <strong>Renderman</strong> <sup id="bibref:19"><a href="#bib:graphics-pixar" role="doc-biblioref">[19]</a></sup>, their pioneering software used for 3D rendering. This was back in the time when 3D graphics were mainly handled by industrial equipment. Later on, we saw how certain consoles incorporated <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#tab-1-1-reality-signal-processor">similar principles</a>, but it wasn’t until Nvidia released their GeForce3 line, that shaders became a standard in the consumer market.</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="tabs nested float-side"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-1-1-vertex-program-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-1-1-vertex-program">Vertex Program</a></li><li id="nestedtab-1-2-pixel-shader-link"><a href="#nestedtab-1-2-pixel-shader">Pixel Shader</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-1-1-vertex-program"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/video_posters/vertex.4ab1783568137eeb45b328dc011837545c4b81b1081f17dedb7b327f4515bae1.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/xbox/vertex.4a74709a770ae9809ad8960e1043cc1287e2527080bac3a44719c618adcae0dc.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Complex animation achieved by vertex program.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-1-2-pixel-shader"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/video_posters/fragment.297261a06dcdc09586458e7a6beb54d1b5f3724b1c0cdf037998075e61af465a.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/xbox/fragment.22636ac1a7696d946b79e1bc90446499b8a456702b4077061deffc7c3858e6c7.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Different texture effects achieved by pixel shaders.</figcaption></figure><figcaption class="caption group">ChameleonMark (2002), a demo developed by Nvidia to showcase GeForce3’s shaders.</figcaption></figure><p>Thanks to vertex programs, the GPU can now accelerate model transformations, lighting calculations and texture coordinate generation. The latter is essential for composing <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-2/#infinite-worlds">Higher Order surfaces</a>. With this, the CPU can concentrate on providing better physics, AI and scene management.</p><p>In the case of pixel shaders, programmers can manipulate and blend textures in multiple ways to achieve different effects such as multi-texturing, specular mapping, bump mapping, environment mapping and so on.</p><p>A new programming concept that emerges thanks to this approach is the <strong>General Purpose GPU</strong> or ‘GPGPU’, which consists of assigning tasks to the GPU that would have been exclusively done by the CPU. So not only the GPU has taken over most of the graphics pipeline, but now can act as an efficient co-processor for specialised computations (i.e. physics calculations). This is a new area that will evolve as GPUs become more powerful and flexible. However, the NV2A was already able to achieve this thanks to a combination of hardware capabilities (vertex & pixel shaders) and specialised APIs developed (OpenGL’s ‘state programs’).</p></div><p>I have a feeling that shaders will be regularly revisited in future articles. Please remember that in this article, however, they may be considered a bit ‘primitive’ and some people may argue that the pixel shaders are not even ‘shaders’ (compared to what GPUs offer nowadays).</p><h3 id="the-xboxs-frame">The Xbox’s frame</h3><p>The standard resolution of games is <strong>640x480</strong>, this is pretty much the standard in the sixth generation. Although, this constraint is just a number: The GPU can draw frame-buffers with up to 4096x4096, yet it doesn’t mean the hardware would provide acceptable performance. On the other side, the console allows configuring its screen setting globally, which may help to promote pioneering features (i.e. widescreen and ‘high resolution’) instead of waiting for developers to discover them (as it happened with the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#tab-1-1-standardised-widescreen">Gamecube/Wii</a>).</p><p>The video encoder, on the other hand, will try to broadcast whatever there is on the frame-buffer in a format your TV will understand. That means that widescreen images will become <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#tab-1-1-standardised-widescreen">anamorphic</a> unless the game outputs in HD (i.e. 720p or 1080i, which only a few games do).</p><p>That being said, what kind of signals does this console broadcast? Quite a lot. Apart from the typical PAL/NTSC composite, the Xbox offers <strong>YPbPr</strong> (requiring an extra accessory to get the ‘component’ connectors) and RGB (both SCART and VGA compliant). All in all, very convenient without requiring expensive adapters and whatnot.</p><hr><h2 id="audio">Audio</h2><p>The audio subsystem of this console was heavily influenced by the technology of professional audio equipment and ATX motherboards, although it does contain some peculiar parts. The MCPX includes two audio components, the <strong>Audio Processing Unit</strong> and the <strong>Audio Controller Interface’</strong>.</p><p>The Audio Processing Unit or ‘APU’ is the dedicated audio processor and is composed of three sub-components:</p><ul><li>The <strong>Voice Processor</strong> or ‘VP’: A specialised circuit that can synthesise 256 voices at a sampling rate of 48 kHz. It also includes two DAHDSR envelope controls and various filters. Furthermore, 64 voices can be 3D (as opposed to Stereo or Mono). At the end, the processor mixes and outputs the voices through 32 channels, where groups of 8 channels have their own volume control.</li><li>The <strong>Global Processor</strong> or ‘GP’: A programmable DSP used to process the audio data from the VP and apply various effects on it.<ul><li>Not all the channels coming from the VP have to be fed here, instead, specific groups can be sent to apply specific effects (i.e reverb) exclusively on them.</li></ul></li><li>The <strong>Encode Processor</strong> or ‘EP’: As the name indicates, it generates the final stereo signal coming from the GP and stores it in main RAM.<ul><li>Notice the operations of the EP can also be carried out by the GP, but having a separate component for encoding enables the console to strive for better audio encoding techniques, such as Dolby Digital.</li></ul></li></ul><p>The APU only processes audio data but can’t output it. The latter is the job of the ACI, which reads the audio data in RAM, decodes it and sends the resulting PCM stereo sample (16-bit resolution with a sampling rate of 48 kHz) through the audio output.</p><hr><h2 id="io">I/O</h2><p>As I mentioned before, we have a ‘Southbridge’ subsystem which concentrates all I/O access. This Southbridge is implemented by the MCPX chip.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/main.be498f7dc9e0c245309ae4e7256ba50a5c317d9164bc6cc8266faf17450aa45b.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="965" height="1071" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/_diagrams/main.be498f7dc9e0c245309ae4e7256ba50a5c317d9164bc6cc8266faf17450aa45b.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Main diagram of the console’s architecture. Notice how the MCPX controls most of the I/O.</figcaption></figure><p>Incidentally, the MCPX derives from its PC counterpart called <strong>nVidia nForce Multimedia and Communications Processor</strong> or ‘MCP’. This is found on motherboards using the nForce 220/415/420 chipset <sup id="bibref:20"><a href="#bib:io-reactos" role="doc-biblioref">[20]</a></sup>.</p><h3 id="external-interfaces">External interfaces</h3><p>The console includes the following external connectors:</p><ul><li><strong>4 USB 1.1 ports</strong>: Used to connect the controllers, however, the external shape of the port is modified to only allow Xbox controllers.<ul><li>These ports also contain an extra pin called ‘Video Sync’ to connect peripherals that interact with the screen.</li></ul></li><li><strong>10/100BASE-TX Ethernet port</strong>: Used for online services (more details later). The actual Ethernet function is performed by a separate transceiver found in the motherboard.</li></ul><h3 id="internal-interfaces">Internal interfaces</h3><p>The MCPX also provides the following interfaces and protocols used to interconnect different subsystems:</p><ul><li><strong>SMBus</strong>: Also referred to as I²C, it’s a serial interface that connects these components:<ul><li><strong>System Management Controller</strong> or ‘SMC’: Manages multiple services, such as power, temperature and fan control. It’s actually a PIC16LC microcontroller.</li><li><strong>System Temperature Monitor</strong> or ‘STM’: A digital thermometer (ADM1032) used by the SMC to detect overheating.</li><li>A <strong>256 B EEPROM</strong>: A re-writable ROM that stores unique identifiers (serial number, region, Ethernet MAC address, etc).</li><li><strong>Video Encoder</strong>: The encoder is primarily connected to the GPU but controlled through the SMBus.</li></ul></li><li><strong>IDE Controller</strong>: This is a standard protocol widely used on PCs to communicate with Hard drives, optical readers and so forth. A single wide ribbon cable is used to connect the motherboard with the DVD drive and the HDD.</li><li><strong>Low Pin Count</strong> or ‘LPC’ bus: This is another interface borrowed from the PC, but instead of connecting the <em>good old</em> PC BIOS, it communicates with a <strong>Flash ROM</strong>, which in turn stores the equivalent of a BIOS. The Flash is <strong>1 MiB</strong> large.</li></ul><h3 id="the-controller">The controller</h3><p>The Xbox came with a bulky controller called <strong>The Duke</strong>, its set of inputs isn’t any different from what the other competitors had… except for the usage of analogue circuitry (8-bit wide) on the face buttons, allowing games to detect ‘half-presses’ from most of the button set. On the other side, the Duke was so widely criticised that Microsoft replaced it with a new revision called <strong>Controller S</strong> months after the release of the console.</p><div class="side-by-side"><figure class="tabs nested toleft"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-2-1-front-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-2-1-front">Front</a></li><li id="nestedtab-2-2-back-link"><a href="#nestedtab-2-2-back">Back</a></li></ul><a class="nested tab active" id="nestedtab-2-1-front" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/controller/duke_front.67de61435d28afa68e0a8a77b13e6812c54c1f14005e99717113b629ea3493e9.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/xbox/controller/duke_front.67de61435d28afa68e0a8a77b13e6812c54c1f14005e99717113b629ea3493e9_hu_4fdbd5367d9aa589.webp 500w,
